utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The witness may be brought in. The Chamber received information about the agreement between Prosecution and Defence on P06670 which was MFI'd. The Prosecution, as I understand, has informed the Defence that it relies on the accompanying transcripts as uploaded into e-court for the video-clip and not on the text shown on the clip itself. And under those circumstances, we understand that the Defence withdraws its objections to the exhibit and, therefore, P06670 is admitted into evidence. We continue with hearing the testimony of Mr Kecmanovic. As I understand, he has agreed or at least he has offered to reappear today rather than later in August or in September. And you needed two sessions, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciated your offer to continue to give your testimony today and that you have given priority to our proceedings over your personal matters. It's highly appreciated. I also would like to remind mind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Lukic will now re-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor. We would like to thank you on our part for delegating your obligations to others. We know it was important to you and we hope that we will complete your examination today. I will start where we left off on Friday when you heard the intercept, and I would like to ask you the following question. Did you have a very sharp tongue and an even more critical pen to all -- when dealing with all three sides?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any difficulties because of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D2993 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will see when this document comes up these were the notices of death for Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, Nikola Koljevic, Ljubo Bosiljcic, Nenad Kecmanovic, Velibor Ostojic, and Nenad Pejic. Which ethnicity are all these people?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991 and 1992, were all these people living?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nenad Kecmanovic mentioned here, who is that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in the -- on the lower left corner of this document. Can you see this? Would you be able to read what it says there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need top part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're unable to make this out, I know that it's difficult to read the B/C/S, but the point is that your death is reported in a sort of pejorative way, making fun of it, correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says that the place of grief has been closed for repair and the place of joy, Zetra, 21, and then it goes on to say who the guests were, the names of Halid Beslic, the red apples, the blue orchestra, Merlin, Oliver Dragojevic, Vera Svoboda, Kico Slabinac, and so on and so forth. Who are these people mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are entertainers, people from show business, singers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you call this a form of PR or propaganda?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would rather define it as a rather tasteless expression of enmity or hostility towards all the people who are mentioned here, and I could also add that this was published in a public paper called "Vox" that was edited by the sons of the Sarajevo mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object as to well for several reasons but primarily relevance. The point of the intercept had to do with the deal that was made in Belgrade. This is not responsive to that point of cross-examination. This also seems to lack any relevance with respect to the matters before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the contrary, we need this document to show what kind of papers were issued in Sarajevo, and what was the atmosphere, and Mr. Donja leaned heavily on Sarajevo newspapers too in his expert analysis. So we think that it's actually one of the crucial documents in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document deals with how people are treated in publications, and the objection is denied. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2933 [sic] receives number D558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D558 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, my learned friend from the Prosecution is now referring to the deal that was agreed in Belgrade. Did you have to be granted any kind of asylum at that time in order to be able to enter Serbia or was anyone able to enter Serbia irrespective of their ethnicity or even the passport?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I could and I went to Belgrade in the meantime on two occasions in fact -- no, actually once during the war, before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you issued any papers, an asylum? Were you made to ask for permission to actually move to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a short moment to clarify the 65 ter number of D558. On the transcript, we have two different numbers, on page 2, line 19, it's 1D2993 and on page 4, line 11 it's 1D2933. Madam Registrar, could you check that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number is 1D2993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see P6658 in e-court, please. Obviously I have a wrong number here. I will get back to this at a later point. So we're not discussing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about your claim relating to the session of the Presidency, about the Serbs shelling the city of Sarajevo indiscriminately. Now, at the sessions of the Presidency, were you informed, in any manner, by the Muslim side where the positions were in the city itself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I only knew this because I had insight into this. That was the only way I learned of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you have been able, then, to know whether the Serbs were actually firing at a military target or whether it was indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they fired actually at two locations near the facilities where I was, and I was able to see those premises at all times. The former command of the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo was one of them. During the war that was the headquarters of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, and this was in the midst of the Ciglana neighbourhood. Now, those people who know the layout of that area will know where that is. Now, the second artillery post was in the tunnel that was at the other end of the Ciglana neighbourhood. The artillery weapons were, in fact, emplaced or placed on a mobile base. They would open fire and then withdraw to the tunnel, and then go -- get out of the tunnel to open fire and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with reference to P6650, that is another record of a session of the Presidency, so I would like to ask you to put the same question in reference to that. We won't pull up the document again but you said there that you were never informed on the BH Army positions at those Presidency sessions. This was only a reference for the Trial Chamber to draw their attention to this document as well. Now, with the assistance of Ms. Stewart, I would like to show an excerpt from the same video that we saw on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution showed you a portion of the video from 9 minutes, 56 seconds, to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request, could you please repeat the references on the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we will see only 47 seconds. From 9 minutes 57 seconds to 10 minutes 43 seconds. [In English] If we can start please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your previous reference was not fully understood by the interpreters, Mr. Lukic. I don't know whether that is repaired by your new reference. Otherwise, please repeat the old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not heard -- the same video from 9 minutes 29 seconds to 9 minutes 56 seconds. And we will just continue where we stopped on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Let's look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we start, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we play it again so that we have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Serious situations call for serious words. How will you prevent everybody from starting killing everybody else in Bosnia and Herzegovina? How can we stop the war in Croatia, especially in the border areas where Serbs and Croats are in contact? Whose two political wills are in conflict and weren't realised in a legal manner which is the only which they should be realised. "From now on, gentlemen, I will ask for the floor on a regular basis until you take this matter of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina off the agenda. That is my right. I want to send a message to Muslims, Serb, and Croatian people that you want to achieve something in Europe that you have no right to. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you said that you understood these words of Mr. Karadzic's as a cautionary note, warning?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you stand by that, even after hearing this portion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would request for a short clip to be shown from this same video, from 5 minutes 57 seconds to 6 minutes 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We kindly request a reference for this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters ask for a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 5 minutes 57 seconds to 6 minutes 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not have those notations on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the transcript the interpreters cannot find it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know it's on the second page in B/C/S. We can have the transcript, but then we won't have this video now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the interpreters would be able to find it, then we could proceed as you started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very, very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the first words so that the interpreters are better able to find the relevant portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No Interpretation] [In English] In B/C/S it's the last third of the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the interpreters have found it. Let's play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry, then I misunderstood the body language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have found it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's watch the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we play it for the second time so we receive the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We can agree not try to stop you, to leave Yugoslavia by using the plebiscite, but through the same plebiscite and the same right we shall prevent you to take us out of Yugoslavia. Here, gentlemen, from the SDA, in our conversations and even in the commission, it was said..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, is this position of President Karadzic, and was that the position of the SDS and of the Serbian side in parliament? Namely, that they didn't want to impose their solution on the other two peoples but that they were just seeking to protect their own right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the difference of a plebiscite of the people and a referendum?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms, it is the same thing. Both terms are used in almost all the media. There are some minor differences but basically it is the same term, practically synonymous.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The mike is not on. Could counsel please turn on his mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown these two slips of paper from the plebiscite, two ballots from the plebiscite of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on the screen T6661 [as interpreted] and T6662 [as interpreted] in B/C/S at the same time on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say T or did you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously we have to wait a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember this? Can you recall this without the ballot slips? Was the question basically the same or was it different?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of content, in terms of substance, the question was exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us continue. On page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it again so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we can have in English maybe just for Your Honours so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that we can compare the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or if it's hard to get both -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think we might be able to manage. If you would just give us time to read the question exactly. Could you explain that, Witness, that asking someone whether he's in favour of a decision already taken is the same as asking someone whether he would -- in favour of a certain thing still to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I could see, the difference between these two ballot slips: In the one which is intended for Serbian, Serb voters, they are invoking the decision of the assembly of the Serbian people which is a preliminary expression of the will of the Serbian people. For voters who are not Serbs, they omitted this part simply because the decision of the Serbian Assembly was not binding in any way whatsoever on these other two peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be any different if you put a question to the population to already include an assumption of a decision being binding or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this actually meant that it was binding on the Serbian people, but just the information that representatives of the Serb people had brought such a decision. And the plebiscite offered the possibility to the Serbian population to also decide otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So these are two different questions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that the questions are the same for both the Serb and the non-Serb voters. Basically the question is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the essence of this question, phrased in two different ways?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the population, the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wished to remain in Yugoslavia or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you done with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put an additional question. Mr. Witness, on the left side, it's referring -- the ballot paper is referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina staying in Yugoslavia as a republic. On the right-hand side, it is the question if the Serb people stay in Yugoslavia, together with other parts of the former Yugoslavia. Is the people, the Serb people, the same as Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please see the original version of the ballot slip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The right-hand side version states that it is the Serbian people because it also refers to the other parts of the Serb people in Slavonia, Baranja, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take from your answer that now you realise that there is a difference between the two, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- there is a difference insofar as it refers to Serb people in Baranja and Slovenia as well as in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, again, on the left side of the screen, isn't it true that this refers only to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not to Serb people in BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is also a difference, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. There is a difference. But simply, it would not be appropriate to put the same question to Serb voters and to Croat voters and to Muslim ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a different question. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for Muslims and Croats to declare themselves in favour of a solution whereby Serbs would remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying whether it had been practically possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could a Muslim vote whether a Serb would remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we agree on the following: That the question that was put to the Serb people was mainly ethnically based, whereas the other one is based more on a state or country or at least a legal entity, whereas -- and that's the main difference, the one referring to ethnicity and the other rather to state institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs were part of that institution too; that is to say, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was not my question. But whether the one text is more ethnically oriented and the other one is more state or country, at least legal entity, oriented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In a certain sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The objective of this plebiscite was -- was it primarily for the Serb people to declare their position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in response to the announced referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was just that the other peoples were also offered an opportunity if they wanted to declare their position. Was that actually the stance of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a reaction to the announcement that Bosnia would gain independence, Serb people were against it, so that the plebiscite was scheduled prior to the referendum in order for the Serb people to declare and to express their will in keeping with the possibilities offered to the other two peoples to express their respective wills.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the objective of this plebiscite to change anything in the constitutional and legal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only to protect the status quo in which Bosnia was part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the page of our transcript, 23897, you were asked whether you had referred in your situation that you had attended the founding Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were there any representatives of any other parties attending the founding assembly apart from SDS representatives?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The founding assembly of the -- the leadership of the SDS invited all parliamentary and I believe even non-parliamentary parties to the founding assembly. The latter as guests. And I was there as the president of the Alliance of Reformist Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was this constitution, this founding of the Serbian Assembly of the people -- of the Assembly of the Serbian People, was this a clandestine act or a public act?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a public act. It actually took place in the building of the parliament in which the joint parliament sat and worked. So it could not have been secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up P6663 to e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document by which the Prosecutor tried to relativise the gravity of the Islamic Declaration, of the words uttered within it. This is a text of an interview with Dr. Vojislav Seselj. My question to you is this: Where was Vojislav Seselj living at this particular moment, prior to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer because the speakers overlapped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer and could you next time wait until the question has been fully interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was Vojislav Seselj living before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you next time refer to questions put by the Prosecution, would you refrain from interpreting on what their goal was just by saying questions were put in relation to or repeat the question but not to characterise it in the way you did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did Vojislav Seselj take part in the political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you mean the period before the war, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please compare his influence on the policies of Bosnia and Herzegovina to those of Alija Izetbegovic's in the time preceding the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic's influence was very significant, very big, both as a leader of the party, the leading party, and also as the president of the Presidency, whereas Seselj was a man living in a different area and he had no direct influence of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know this? Did the Serb politicians request that Alija Izetbegovic renounce his positions as set forth in the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs and Croats, asked Alija Izetbegovic to renounce the positions that he set out in the Islamic Declaration after the republication of this pamphlet in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now pull up P6664, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it, could I ask the following question: Mr Kecmanovic, you were asked a question about the influence of Mr. Seselj on politics in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your answer was about the direct influence. Does that mean that indirectly he may have had influence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that he may have had some influence on people who went to Belgrade maybe and sought his activities there, because this was still one integral country and people could move freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question about influence should be answered by he may have had influence but that was not direct political influence. Is that how I have to understand your answer now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps one could say that his influence was not relevant because he was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself and he did not take part in the political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had no public office there, didn't hold any public office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has ever any study been made about his unofficial or his factual influence on the way of thinking in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of anything like that existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I therefore understand it it's your subjective impression on the influence that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the result of what I knew about the situation in pre-war Sarajevo and what I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the lower left part of this document to be zoomed in on. This is a reference to we will call on our members to vote in the referendum. It is very difficult to read this in the original, so I will try to help. The Prosecutor read out half a sentence from this excerpt, from this text by you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's almost impossible to decipher this. I had to refer to the English version and read it back as it were. So that's how I will do it now and you will receive interpretation into B/C/S. The Prosecutor read out the following portion of the sentence: [In English] "The radical circles of the SDS Serbian Democratic Party are seeking to sever parts of B and H with a predominantly Serbian population from the republic and establish new states?" [Interpretation] A question followed after that, and now I will go on and read out what you said next. [In English] "Whereas the extremist factions within the HDZ, following the same principle, wished to attach the appropriate territories to the Independent State of Croatia. In the same vein, like-minded factions in the SDA, party of democratic action, are seeking to ensure predominance for their own relatively mostly numerous ethnic group within a unitary Bosnia." [Interpretation] So we see here that the radical wing, and that's what you explained, on page 23906 of the transcript of 11 July 2014, you explained that this comment here is a reference to the extremists, not the fundamental policies of that party. In other words, it's about the radical wing of the HDZ. Now, my question is this: The radical wing of the HDZ was doing the same thing as the radical wing of the SDS. Could you describe in brief here the difference between those, the radical wing of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the difference is in that the Muslims, at this time, as well as Bosniaks to this day, insist on the unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina outside of Yugoslavia, and then from the ultra-unitarian, ultra-centralised, that if it was set up that way, it would automatically mean that the other two ethnicities would be less equal because they were minorities. This problem has existed throughout this entire period, from the period leading up to the war up to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, the SDA radical wing, was Alija Izetbegovic a member of this radical wing as the head of the party? In other words, was that also his position, that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be unitarised?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Alija Izetbegovic, on several occasions one could get the impression that he was willing to compromise. For instance, that was the case with the Lisbon Agreement as well as in some other occasions, also the Belgrade historic meeting. So in the beginning he demonstrated readiness for compromise, but as this changed, there were assumptions that there were some extremist factors within the parties that would then exert pressure on him and then he would pull back from what he had offered previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P6666.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the final analysis, he did stand up for these radical positions, regardless of whether that was under the influence of other wings, other circles, or whether it was his own position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this subsequent explanation. Now we can see document P6666, and it was put to you that Krajisnik had said we've always considered the partition or division of Sarajevo. Do you know which settlements and which populations were supposed to remain under Serbian control? Was that -- was it the case that these were settlements or neighbourhoods with Serb populations or did they feel that they should control the Muslim settlements and neighbourhoods as well?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, is this the conversation between Krajisnik and Izetbegovic? Is that what this text is reference to, this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a meeting that I attended myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't see your name here.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any case, the Serbian positions around Sarajevo, military positions, were on territories around Sarajevo that were Serbian territories before the war. The outskirts of Sarajevo, or rather the surroundings of Sarajevo, those were areas where Serb people lived before the war. Or to put it even more precisely, the majority of the populations there were majorities were Serbian, nothing was really ethnically completely pure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I ask one -- a couple of short questions. Would you agree that the Serbs feared a situation where they became a minority in an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the party that I was the head of, and that means that my personal position as well as that of the party, which was called the Alliance of Reformist Forces of Yugoslavia, and it retained that name until the end, we advocated the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we -- and Yugoslavia, because we felt that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not viable without the Yugoslav surroundings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to another question, not mine. The -- I repeat then the question: Would you agree that the Serbs, and I add now that the prevalent position of the Serbs was that they feared a situation where they became a minority if Bosnia-Herzegovina would become independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be more specific in your question? The thing is Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were a relative minority even before the war within Yugoslavia, within the Yugoslav context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, that was not my question but if you rather -- I think my question was clear: Did most of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina fear to end up in a minority position if Bosnia and Herzegovina would become independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that Serbs had such anxieties, in view of the experience of Serbs in Croatia, where, from a constituent ethnicity, they suddenly were turned into a minority which was how it was formulated in the new constitution, and it's quite certain that there were such fears among Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you think that or did you observe that Muslims had fear to remain a minority in the situation where Bosnia and Herzegovina remained a part of the federal republic, a minority meaning a minority in the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were such fears. That's sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although -- I apologise. A majority of the Muslim people, a large majority, lived in this portion of Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, some in Serbia, and in Macedonia and Montenegro. A large majority of the Muslims were in this part of Yugoslavia so that their numbers would not be significantly altered, and even in this rump Yugoslavia the structure would have been such that the Muslim ethnicity would be the second-largest ethnicity, whereas in the former Yugoslavia they were the third-largest ethnicity. But in this rump Yugoslavia they would have been the second-largest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that fear for ending up in a minority position, either in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as the Serbs are concerned, or for the Muslims to remain a minority in the federal republic, was prevalent among both ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take Yugoslavia as a whole, the pre-war Yugoslavia, as I've already said, the Serbs were the largest ethnic group, the Croats were the second, whereas the third -- the Muslims were the third largest. Now in Yugoslavia without Slovenia and Croatia, the Muslims would have been the second largest, so they would have actually gone up from third place to second place in this truncated Yugoslavia. Now that there were fears that you mention, there is no doubt about that because I've heard people voice such fears. When I talked with Alija Izetbegovic on this subject, he did not show any reserve to such a community, which would have been in line with so-called historic agreement that Zulfikarpasic advocated. But when I mentioned this alternative and when I mentioned that after Milosevic he would have been the next president of this joint state, this was that -- this was a portion of that agreement, and this is where he expressed certain doubts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Doubts as to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, doubts that he would have been the next president, the first president of this new state. However, that was Milosevic's proposal. It was on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he fear, because the Muslims not having a majority vote in the federal republic, that he might finally not be appointed as president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I assume that he thought that Zulfikarpasic would have an advantage there. He was the main proponent of this historic agreement; in other words, that Bosnia should remain in this rump Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, it was then fear for his own position that led Izetbegovic to advocate the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this was a broad -- these were broad, informal talks, where we discussed his position vis-à-vis Serbia and Croatia and Milosevic and Tudjman. He simply felt, considered, that in the final analysis, Bosnia and Herzegovina should be independent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether the witness said "should" or "shouldn't."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you say should be independent or should not be independent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He considered that it should be independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for an answer which, by the way, was not an answer to my question. Please proceed. But it's already far beyond the time where we should have taken a break. We take a break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I shall go back to the question which was put to you by His Honour Judge Orie. On page 23, line 19, I shall read it in English so that you would get the correct interpretation. I quote: [In English] "If I understand you well, it was then fear for his own position that led Izetbegovic to advocate the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" [Interpretation] Let me just expand upon this particular question. Did this, in with your opinion, at all influence? Was this the sole reason? Were there other reasons? Was this one of the reasons? Please reply.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that it was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's a little late now that the witness has answered, but I wonder if we could have one question at a time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you'll certainly take this as guidance for next questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was really -- what I wanted to do was to ask a simple question for the Professor to answer, but I will just ask another associated question. Was this the principal reason or were there some other reasons which were more important for him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the reason was the fact that he wanted an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which again is not an answer to the question. But please move on because the question was about what was the reason. And what the witness answered was what the aim was, and reason and aim is not the same. But please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would this objective at the same time be a reason for Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The confusion continues. Please proceed. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on. [Interpretation] Can we now please see 65 ter 30941. That is an OTP document. Actually, that is the transcript from the Krajisnik case. And we need page 142 which was also used by the Prosecutor for their question and that corresponds to transcript number 22465. That's actually the transcript page number, 22465.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you recall, this is the conversation which was relayed to you by your wife. I'll read you from where we left off, so from line 17 to line 20. That is a continuation, and I'm quoting: [In English] "My wife recounted that conversation and said she had told him that I certainly wouldn't do anything that would be to the detriment of the Serb people, as I would not indeed do anything to the detriment of any other people." [Interpretation] This position which was related to them by your wife, does it really reflect your position in both life and in politics, your political position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this Presidency in Sarajevo, at the outset of the war, the members who were from among the ranks of the Croatian people, would they be co-opted or would they be elected representatives who had been elected at pre-war elections?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was a member of the Presidency, they were elected representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have concluded with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P6667 called in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These are obviously minutes of meeting from a Presidency session the Prosecutor showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need page 3 in the English version and page 4 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page, Akmadzic is saying, referring to the negotiations being conducted by the presidents of -- Presidency of the B and H that lead to peace, and he also talks about the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we need the following page, in fact, page 5 in the B/C/S version and page 4 in the English version. In the middle of the page, you talk and you say at the end of the paragraph that no changes whatsoever will be accepted in the national structure of the population that have produced by the war, by the moving away of people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with this part, the Prosecutor suggested to you that it would not be accepted -- that they would not be accepted because a genocide had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is page 23932 of our transcript of the 11th of July 2014, lines 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the record, the word "genocide" comes from a different excerpt, not from this excerpt, and so I think the question may create more confusion in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, possibly I mixed up two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But on page 23932 of our transcript of the 11th of July, the Prosecutor asked you, that is lines 3 to 4, and you replied, I'll read it all through to line 10 and you will be getting the interpretation. I quote: [In English] "Those are territorial ethnic changes caused by violence, war, genocide, moving away, et cetera." "A. Yes, yes. "Q. That's you speaking, right? "A. Yes. "Q. And you knew at that time that changes in the ethnic makeup of Bosnia-Herzegovina were happening for all these reasons? "A. Yes." [Interpretation] You have already explained that while you were a member of the Presidency in Sarajevo, you would adopt conclusions pursuant to reports on everything that related to the situation outside Sarajevo. And then later, on page of the transcript 23828 of 10 July 2014, line 25, this is what you said, and I quote: [In English] "I cannot take into account as relevant information that I received as member of the Presidency because those information were sort of wartime propaganda." [Interpretation] Was everything that you said at sessions of the Presidency of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for things which emanated from Sarajevo, was that -- was everything based on information that you received within the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, that was the information that you later characterised as being war propaganda?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also told us that reference was made -- actually claims were made about 300.000 Muslims have been killed in the first months of the war. That was part of that propaganda. Was this information that came only from foreign media or was such information also imparted at Presidency sessions that were chaired by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both sources coincided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P6669 in e-court now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is hardly legible but let us try and see the second paragraph from the top of the second column. This was also presented to you by the Prosecutor. [In English] On the right-hand side to the end of the page, please. All the way. Yes. And the second paragraph from the top. Yes. [Interpretation] At any rate, you don't even have to read this. You talk about who should be given what portion of territory, what percentage of territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you of course took account the population numbers or the fact that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there existed three constituent peoples, and in this text you concluded that the Serbs should be given a third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is the equivalent English paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had it but somehow I lost the reference in English. Probably it's the next page in English version, under the title: "The Split is -- was Inevitable." On the right-hand side. Top of the page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In presenting your view here, did you take into account the ownership of territory or property that was in the hands of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the 1990s war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a principled position, from the standpoint justice. However, it was not only a question of landownership but also a question of the concentration of the population on specific territories. Of course, the picture would not be literally such because the Muslims were concentrated in cities, whereas the Serbs for the most part lived in rural areas. So -- and the result of the Dayton Accords is also that because of that, the Muslims were given the majority of the big cities, such as Sarajevo, Tuzla, Mostar, and the Serbs only got Banja Luka, when it came to the major cities. We are talking about a principle of justice here, of equity, and we are also talking about something which is associated with 1992, that particular year. Later, things unfolded in a different manner. The war went on and new situations emerged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, did we have the proper B/C/S page on our screen at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I'm lost somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's hardly visible so even I cannot follow. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But where exactly -- what's the English text we are looking at at this moment exactly? You said under "The Split is or was Inevitable," which paragraph in that? The first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a question, the last question on the screen: "Do have you a personal position on the criteria according to which" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- "that split should be carried out," and then the answer followed underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next text which was used by the OTP from this particular document is in the middle of the page at the bottom, English page 3, [In English] And we need bottom of the page, "Everyone ...," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S we have to go down. No, we need aggressor and aggressors. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English, that's page 4, in English e-court page 4. I think where it reads "aggressors and aggressors" between brackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. In English I have right page. In B/C/S I need page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- and what is the text then in English you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Everyone to his own Crowd."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1. We need page 2 in B/C/S. Next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we have page 3 in English now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the middle -- just above, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Each to his own or Everyone to his own Crowd." At the time when you were interviewed, did you consider the reasons why people were leaving one territory only to go to another? Did you interview them? Did you know the reasons that people -- what reasons people were guided by when they were leaving the territories?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What conclusions could you draw? Why were they leaving?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People fled the conflict, the war. They tried to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Belgrade, I met people, not Croats but Serbs and Muslims, large numbers of Serbs and Muslims, some remained there and others only used Belgrade as a stepping stone to leave to a foreign country. They were fleeing the war. They were fleeing the threat to their life, the insecurity, their concern for their children. Those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you had occasion to talk with these people in Belgrade. Did you have an opportunity to speak to some people who told you that they were expelled, that they were forced out of their own homes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were probably such instances too, individual cases, but for the most part it was the fear of the threat lurking and the fear that the situation would exacerbate, just as it had gotten worse in the past period. There were warnings by friends and neighbours, they would get information of certain nature, and these were the reasons, the primary reasons, why they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question? In your interview, at least as far as I could read, the issue is not people fleeing Bosnia and Herzegovina but rather the territories where they apparently were in a minority. Do I have to understand in view of your latest answers that most of them fled to outside the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not inside the borders to Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such cases as well but of course I didn't meet those people in Belgrade. And the question related to Belgrade, my experience in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which might not have been a representative portion of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, to explain why people fled focusing on what may have been a smaller number that fled to Belgrade may create a -- at least a partial picture only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, a portion of the population left, and I mentioned that in this interview, in fact everyone left for the territories where their own ethnicity was dominant. This was one of the ways in which they sought safety and security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within or outside Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, people -- during the war people within Bosnia-Herzegovina also gravitated towards the territories where most of their own ethnicity lived. Some of them left for Belgrade. Some remained in Serbia. And others just went to third countries via Belgrade. Many left for Canada and Australia. For instance, my brother and his family, they left for Australia via Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you talk about three categories. Those who stayed in Serbia, those who went to third countries, you said -- let me see. You said some of them left for Belgrade, some remained in Serbia, and others just went to third countries. I asked you about those who remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's not one of the three categories you are specifying. But let's move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Traldi asked you something that has to do with paragraph 55 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would request that we have 1D1633 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now D556.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number is 1663.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we need paragraph 55 from your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the mid-section of that paragraph, at the end of the line which begins with, "also" or "takodzer," which is the easiest way to find it in B/C/S. [In English] And in English it says in the middle of the paragraph: "I also believe that it was possible." [Interpretation] So the sentence reads as follows: "I also believe it was possible to transform Bosnia-Herzegovina territorially and ethnically without any radical or forced changes to the ethnic structure on the ground." On transcript page 23943, my learned friend Traldi put the following question from lines 15 to 19 and you answered on line 20 the following, and I will read it out now: [In English] "Q. Sir, I'd put to you that in your statement you are saying it was possible to do this when you know and you said publicly at that time that what actually happened was that the ethnic composition of Bosnia was transformed in a completely different way through violence, through war, through genocide. That's right, isn't it? "A. Yes." [Interpretation] Sometimes in long questions, there are certain omissions and they may be very important to us lawyers. Did you intend to mention the word "genocide" in your statement and would you change that as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an omission, certainly. I wouldn't have mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- first of all, let me ask you this: Do you know what the definition of genocide is?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way it's used today, at least, when we talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is quite different from what genocide used to be interpreted as, both in theory and practice, because the word "genocide" meant the systematic destruction of a people that can be likened to what the Nazis did to the Jews. And this is not applicable to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where neither one of the peoples intended to totally destroy the other people, the other ethnicity. There are of course some other interpretations of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you P6671. These are the minutes of the 14th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 3rd of July 1992. You were -- it was -- item 12 was put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we would need the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already talked about this, and it is indisputable that the Serbian politicians were dissatisfied with your participation. You explained why you remained. It was for the benefit of the Serbs who were still in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would just like to make a comment here. And I haven't found that anywhere in any of the documents or materials other than my mention of it in my statement. The SDS position was that I did not have the right to represent the Serbian people. Never in my work in the Presidency, and also when I communicated with international partners, I never said that I was a representative of the Serbian people. On the contrary, I even mentioned -- I stated clearly to Cutileiro and Carrington that I was not a representative of the Serbian people, and Cutileiro in his later statement to the media pointed this out. He emphasised that I said that if he wanted to talk to the Serbian side, he would have to go to Pale and discuss matters with Karadzic and not with me. And Karadzic mentioned this in his statement later on when giving an interview to Crna, and he pointed out that it was fair of me to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You've actually already answered a lot of my questions. You anticipated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This only for the transcript. This also relates to P6672, which is also a record of a session of the Presidency on the 6th of July, the 15th Session of 6 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to go back to what we discussed on Thursday. First I wanted to go through the questions and answers on Friday, but now I would like to go back to Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need P6657 for this. Thank you. These are minutes of a Presidency session chaired by Alija Izetbegovic on the 30th of June 1992. And just as the Prosecutor did, I would like page 7 in the English version and 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see here, and I will just summarise this, that you complained that you can no longer do your job because of all the numerous calls and requests to explore where people had been taken, how long they would be kept and why, and you say, in spite of my personal interventions, both with the military and the police and so on, and you said, I am not asking for anything to be done this way or that, but just to have established where people are and why and for how long they would be kept because this has become a very large-scale problem. Now, you've explained that this had to do with the Serbs who had been taken or captured and taken away in Sarajevo, who were held in Sarajevo. And my colleague Traldi, referring to this, asked you whether you briefed the Presidency that there was a detention facility for Muslims that was on territory under control -- under the control of the Serbian BH. The Army of Republika Srpska. And you said that you didn't have such information and I would like to ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's a translation issue which is why I'm hesitant to term this an objection, but I think that misstates the question I asked the witness, and I don't think I asked him if he briefed the Presidency about that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked the witness whether in his statement he mentioned that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I asked him whether he mentioned the detention facilities for Muslims in Serb-controlled territory in his statement, right, not whether he had briefed the Presidency about them. That was the only clarification to the record I was seeking, and to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I remember this well? You said that you didn't know anything about that at the time, and that you don't have any personal knowledge of any detention centres for Muslims and Croats on a Serb-held territories?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, I would actually like to focus on this document in my questions. At the Presidency sessions, did the Muslim representatives inform you about detention facilities or camps for Serbs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got that information from citizens and I've mentioned that. There were lines almost of people waiting to complain to me about what had happened to their loved ones, and then after those complaints I intervened directly and I spoke with the military and the civilian police in an effort to get some kind of resolution. But knowing from after -- after a lot of these instances and after the experience that I had with this, I informed the Presidency at one point of all these things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I see in English that we have Mr. Izetbegovic's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see Mr. Izetbegovic talking here in the middle of the page. At the end of that paragraph, that is the fourth line from the bottom, it starts with, "This was Todje [phoen]." In response to your warnings, your comments, President Izetbegovic says it was some sort of house arrest or questioning. It is not prison. My question to you is this: According to reports from citizens, according to what you tried to detect in the hotels, the Hotel Europa and I forgot the name of the other one, Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zagreb. And then the Mladen Stojanovic Students' Hostel. That was also president --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that house arrest or was that prison?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if someone is in house arrest they remain in their own house and they are confined to their own houses or flats in terms of movement, but in this case they were taken away at night and none of their family members or any of their relatives knew where they were. And this was a large-scale practice. It was on a massive scale. Some of them never returned, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of Sefer Halilovic when you mentioned the military police to him? Did he try to explain or to intervene, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've been patient, but I'm not sure how this part of the line of questioning arises from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It arises from the document that the Prosecution offered into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not the same as arising from -- if every link of any document which is used in a specific way could be sufficient to start re-examination on those matters, then we would be here with this witness until Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, this is the only witness we have from that Presidency. We have nobody else to ask. And I don't have many questions left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but -- no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but whom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one would have prevented you from --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one would have prevented you from putting those questions to this witness in the examination-in-chief, and let's -- this is the last question, then. The witness may answer the question but you're expected then to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You replied but it is not in the transcript. Maybe that is the better because my learned friend Traldi had an objection. But with His Honour's leave I shall repeat the question and we shall conclude with that topic. So I asked you what was the reaction of Sefer Halilovic when you referred to the fact that the military police too were participating in these detentions? Did he try to explain that? Did he try to intervene? Or what, if you know.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He actually disregarded these complaints. It was Izetbegovic who, for the most part, reacted. Actually, I think that these structures were not under Sefer Halilovic's control at all. That was directly associated with Izetbegovic and his two key associates who in formal terms did not hold any state offices, such as Hasan Cengic, who was in charge for the party, for the military sector, on behalf of the party. And then Bakir Alispahic who held a lower-ranking position in the Sarajevo MUP but he was actually the SDA or Izetbegovic's commissioner for internal affairs, for the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked, although there was some objections, how Sefer Halilovic responded. You said he ignored it. That's an answer to the question. You were not asked to tell us the context, et cetera. Mr. Lukic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give me one second. I'm closing to the end. So I should maybe inform everybody that I don't have many questions left, just one minute so I can go through the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time. Not too much but take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just go through one more document and I think that I will then finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have on our screens P6659.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from July 1992. In connection with this document, the OTP put to you the second page in both versions. We do not need it, but the question put to you by the Prosecutor was if you knew who Mico Stanisic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we need actually is page 8 in both versions, which was the one referred to subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph was read out to you where it is stated that the army and the Crisis Staffs, the War Presidencies, are asking for as many Muslim inhabitants to be collected, and they leave such undefined camps to the organs of the interior. The conditions in these camps are bad, not in terms of food, sometimes individuals do not respect international norms because, inter alia, such collection centres are not adequate or there are other reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter has translated it from the original. Not -- cannot see the exact paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please look at the observation by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I might assist, I think due to the correction to the English translation, the text Mr. Lukic is looking for may appear on page 7 now in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, let's try. I was working with probably another version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I think he's looking for the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this assist the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, do you have any knowledge about the actual competences, the ambits, who was in charge of which collection centre, whether there was an overlapping of such competencies, do you have any knowledge about that or did you at all deal with that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you don't, but let me ask you do you have any firsthand knowledge, personal knowledge, which are related to these centres that you could testify about as a fact witness?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What centres are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, where the witness said that he has no knowledge, because that's what you asked him, do you have any knowledge about that or did you at all deal with that? No. I understood that to be that he has no knowledge and did not deal with it. And then to ask him whether he has any firsthand knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No knowledge includes firsthand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, that was -- that was everything I had for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, thank you for staying with us for longer than we told you would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, I'd like to ask one clarification on one issue. You were asked about the propaganda, and you said that on the radio, for instance, you heard about 300.000 Muslim casualties as early in the first few months of the war. But you added to that, if you remember correctly. Now, this Chamber was presented by the Prosecution with a telephone conversation between Mr. Karadzic and certain Mr. Djoko or -- in which he would have said -- Gojko Djoko, in which he would have said that there are 4.000 armed Serbs in Bosnia, 20.000 of them in Sarajevo, and that Sarajevo itself will become a cauldron where 300.000 Muslims will die. That is the only reference, but I may be mistaken, where the number of 300.000 appears but then it's not from media sources but from a telephone conversation. Could you tell us where you said if I -- you remember accurately, where did you find the 300.000 in the international media? And if the parties could assist in pointing at any publication where a number of 300.000 is mentioned, that of course the Chamber would appreciate as well, but, first, you seem not to be certain about it. Could you give us a bit more explanation as where your doubts are and where you may have found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me after more than 20 years to be very specific, to tell you precisely what way. This was a project that was referred to in talks among people in Sarajevo, and they referred to it as something that had been aired or carried by the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said that appeared in the media, you intended to say that people said that it appeared in the media. You didn't see it yourself in the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I heard it both personally and from other people, but I cannot tell you exactly what particular medium. At any rate, it was on the radio, not television, and not the press because the press didn't practically exist any longer at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were talking about international media. The international media did continue to exist, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understood your line, if you remember accurately, not only to be about what source, because you were not very specific on that, but also on the number. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reference was made to about 300.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We will take a break and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Mr. Traldi, would you have any questions for the witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be probably 10 to 15 minutes but I'll be able to be more accurate after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Accuracy on numbers is always appreciated. Then we first take that break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Traldi will have some more questions for you. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, sir, at temporary transcript page 15 today, you asserted that Mr. Seselj did not take part in the political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war. Now, Seselj did speak, did give political speeches, in Bosnia regularly before the war, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj left for Belgrade a number of years before the war, and he lived there. As for Sarajevo, as far as I know, he did not go to Sarajevo before the war.
