utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, so the Trial Chamber has received evidence that Mr. Seselj, for instance, gave speeches in Pale -

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I refer to P319.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- and met repeatedly with Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I refer to P5129.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: --- in the spring of 1991. Were you aware of any of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a talk show on TV, supposed to be. He was supposed to appear in that show, but that was cancelled. As for the meetings at Pale, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And about the meetings with Mr. Karadzic which was part of the question as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As of the spring of 1991, Mr. Karadzic was the leader of the SDS, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj's political party, the Serbian Radical Party, were you aware of that party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, it published a magazine called "Velika Serbia," which was distributed in Bosnia in 1991. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am aware of that publication, but I didn't know that it was distributed, at least it wasn't in Sarajevo, or I don't know that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in light of that information, would you agree that meeting with the leader of the SDS, giving political speeches, and publishing a political magazine, does, in fact, constitute participating in the political life of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Seselj is a colleague and a friend, and I met with him in Belgrade. I knew what his positions were, but that didn't have any effect on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think you've answered a different question than the one I asked. I hadn't asked about your personal relationship with Mr. Seselj. What I'd asked was whether you agree that if you give political speeches in Bosnia, you publish a political magazine in Bosnia, and you meet with political leaders in Bosnia, you are participating in the political life of Bosnia. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we be more precise? He didn't publish in Bosnia. That was published in Serbia. Perhaps that was an omission on your part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the -- Mr. Kecmanovic, what about carefully listening? I think that Mr. Traldi talked about distribution in, not publishing in. So therefore, to comment and to suggest that it was an omission on his part, rather listen carefully. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would it assist if I repeated the question? And I see you've nodded but you have to articulate your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you agree that if you give political speeches in Bosnia, you publish a political magazine which is distributed in Bosnia, and you meet with political leaders in Bosnia, you are participating in the political life of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirectly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir, Mr. Lukic suggested to you today at page 28 that your comments in Presidency meetings were based on propaganda that you received in Presidency meetings. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified at page 28 that everything you said at Presidency meetings was based on information you received within the Presidency. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise? I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If it would assist, if you give me a moment, I can read back the question and answer. You were asked at line 15, beginning on line 15: "Was everything that you said at sessions of the Presidency of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for things which emanated from Sarajevo, was that -- was everything based on information that you received within the Presidency?" And you answered: "Yes." Does that refresh your recollection as to the question you were asked today?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, there was some discussion on Thursday as to whether and when you relied upon the reports you received as a member of the Presidency. And you said, for instance, at transcript page 23829: "None of us could really rely upon what we were -- kept hearing in Presidency meetings." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at T 23833 you testified that you showed confidence in Presidency reports when they corresponded with information you received from other sources such as the media. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then perhaps I wasn't precise enough. The media reports were for the most part identical to what I heard in -- at the Presidency meetings. Perhaps the best way to put it would be that I received information selectively based on my own assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We looked at reports you received in the Presidency which related to city-wide shelling and ethnic cleansing. Similar information appears in your expert reports, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the shelling of the city, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Also about ethnic cleansing, right, in various territories in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was information within the Presidency, that we received within the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified on Thursday that you hadn't relied on information from within the Presidency in drafting your expert reports. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, selectively, as I've already said. Some information was believable, and then I would cross check them with others, but I can't really be very precise in my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So where we've seen information in your expert reports that matches what you were receiving in the Presidency, that reflects either that you found it believable or that you'd cross-checked it with other sources and found it corroborated, correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I want to just look at one quick document before we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 14958.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As this comes up, at temporary transcript page 3 today, Mr. Lukic showed you a publication that you described as expressing enmity or hostility towards you from the Muslim side. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the release of the English translation is of some concern to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. President, and I would just ask -- I think it should be remedied now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the English translation is an empty page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Fortunately we have video of the same thing so it might be simplest to just play that. Let me see if Ms. Stewart is able to do that quickly. And I believe we'll have to play it twice. It has not been pre-confirmed. The 65 ter for the record is 30952A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the person would have been in the courtroom, I would have asked him to slow down. But let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "President of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, also reacted to the news we just broadcast that Mr Kecmanovic and Mirko Pejanovic became members of the Croatian Muslim coalition; that is, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He said Messrs Nenad Kecmanovic and Mirko Pejanovic have been selected in private and in secret and have become Alija Izetbegovic's own private Serbs. "Dr. Radovan Karadzic gave this statement to a 'Tanjug' Yugoslav news agency reporter today. In the statement carried by the Serbian agency 'Crna,' Karadzic made the comment on the occasion of Kecmanovic and Pejanovic being selected into the Presidency. He said, Karadzic, that it is a sad fact the two have become Alija Izetbegovic's own private Serbs. "'Ante Pavelic also had his own private Serbs and Franjo Tudjman has them also,' added the President of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 'They are Izetbegovic's own private Serbs on account of the fact that they represent no one but themselves because the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina have chosen their representatives and at the plebiscite they decided they do not want to live in Alija Izetbegovic's state. The Serbian people are continuing their journey in their free state and we wish the two a safe journey in Alija Izetbegovic's Jamahiriya,' said Dr. Radovan Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a response to you joining the Izetbegovic Presidency. Ante Pavelic was the Croatian Ustasha leader during the Second World War, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of people were murdered by his forces, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Comparing you to Serbs who collaborated with Pavelic was a very serious accusation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that, "Many Serbs, especially the general membership of the SDS, saw Mirko Pejanovic and myself as traitors. However, I think that was partly a result of propaganda for the general public and that the SDS leadership, whose representatives knew me well, did not think of me that way." This statement by Mr. Karadzic is, in fact, an example of just the kind of propaganda you're describing in your statement, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 30952A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30952A receives number P6674, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6674 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also -- we are at the conclusion of your testimony, Mr Kecmanovic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and I repeat my appreciation for you making yourself available today so as to be able to conclude your -- hearing your testimony. And I'd like to wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, now that the witness has been escorted out I'd ask that Mr. Lukic and myself also be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good that the Prosecution requests Mr. Lukic to be excused. It underlines the relations between Prosecution and Defence. At least in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe it was -- I believe I'm simply returning the courtesy he showed me last time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that again underlines the same. You are excused, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness -- is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour, and I understand he should be in the building already. It's Colonel Milorad Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Without -- no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sehovac. Before you give evidence the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehovac. Please be seated. Mr. Sehovac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic, you'll find him to your left, standing. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, with the assistance of the usher, I would provide the witness a clean copy of his statement in printed form. And at the same time, then I would call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D01626. And, sir, directing your attention to the Serbian copy on the left, can you confirm for us whose signature is present?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to the last page of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, sir, once that page comes up, I direct your attention to the Serbian on the left. And could you tell us whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That is my signature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this statement for the Defence team of General Mladic, did you have occasion to review the same in the Serbian language during proofing with myself?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to call up 65 ter number 1D02834 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment. If I can have one moment, Your Honour, I'm trying to resolve this issue. If you try again, I think it should be 1D02834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is unable to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm advised it's also near the break -- time for a break. Perhaps we could have a break and I will try to get this proofing note issue resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is not. But nevertheless, it may be a practical solution to take the break now so that you are fully organised and we have then another 50 minutes after the break. So we take a break pretty earlier than we would expect and then resume in 20 minutes from now. Witness, we first have to overcome some practical problems. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We take a break first, and then you'll be in court for another 50 minutes today to answer any further questions. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if I understand well, you were not fully able to resolve the problem but we will find a practical way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although at this moment that would prevent us from any formal admission of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, called information report. It also says confidential. Is there any -- if I've got the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the same. I don't think there is anything confidential in it. The statement itself is public, so I don't think there is any reason, apart from the fact that it was informally sent, for it to remain confidential and not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Madam Registrar, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen we have what is -- what corresponds to 1D02834. Is this -- is this a copy of the corrections and clarifications that you prepared with me this past week and weekend to your written statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to review all of the corrections and clarifications listed here in the Serbian language such that you can confirm their completeness and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. And I stand by all of this and I had occasion to read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the corrections that are listed in this written document, do you stand behind the rest of your written statement 1D01626, of which you have a hard copy in front of you, as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps now if we can call up 1D01626 and go again to the first page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to ask you these same questions today about the same topics that are contained in your statement, would your answers in substance be identical to those contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: In essence they would be identical and they wouldn't change anything significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Having taken the solemn declaration today to tell the truth, would these answers, as contained in your statement, be truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the written statement 1D01626 into evidence, and I would ask for 1D02834 to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1626 receives number D559, and document 1D2834 receives number D560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: MFI, I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it receives that number and it's marked for identification. So D559 is admitted into evidence and D560 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And, Your Honours, I would leave the associated exhibits until the end of this witness, and at this time I'm prepared to read the summary pursuant to Rule 92 ter which has been explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, as suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milorad Sehovac was commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade of the VRS from 18 August 1992 onwards. His testimony is that the ABiH 1st Corps in Sarajevo had 44.000 to 64.000 soldiers in the city itself. Together with the units outside the city, the ABiH numbered 100.000 soldiers in the Sarajevo theatre of war. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps by comparison had 22.000 to 25.000 soldiers. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had two objectives: To protect the territory and to protect the population. And towards that end, tried to blockade the forces of the ABiH 1st Corps in Sarajevo. When carrying out combat operations, opening fire, or returning fire that came from Sarajevo, neither his brigade nor Colonel Sehovac viewed these actions as part of a systematic attack on civilians. He heard about offers made by the VRS Main Staff and civilian authorities for Sarajevo to become a demilitarised city. Superior commands informed his brigade about the provisions of the international law of war and humanitarian law. During the war, the brigade educated officers, junior officers, and soldiers alike through various forms of training, the most common of which were printed brochures, meetings, and talks by the assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs. It was stressed and ordered by military and political leaders that one was to act and accord with the Geneva Conventions. There were no exclusively civilian zones in neither Hrasnica nor Dobrinja in which the ABiH did not have firing positions or forces located. Colonel Sehovac's brigade took precautionary measures to avoid opening fire on civilian facilities. Neither he nor his superiors ever ordered for attacks to be conducted against civilians. Efforts were undertaken by his brigade to try and reduce collateral casualties among civilians when firing upon ABiH positions. There were no paramilitaries in his zone of responsibility. The witness knows that General Mladic was vigorously opposed to paramilitaries. As to snipers, the witness states he did not have specially organised sniper units in his brigade. All snipers were trained and neither the brigade command nor the witness had any information that snipers were being tasked to open fire on civilians in Sarajevo. Snipers were exclusively tasked with engaging military targets of the enemy. As far as the casualties of his brigade are concerned, due to the unfavourable tactical position of his brigade, and constant offensive operations by the enemy, one in eight of his soldiers was killed and one in three of his soldiers was wounded. That completes the summary. I would now move on to some follow-up questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 in both versions of the statement and focus on paragraph 6 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here you have identified active defensive operations and active combat on the part of your brigade. What are these terms to be understood as covering?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Active combat operations means attacks by parts of the brigade against elements of the combat disposition of the enemy that is attacking. Usually these would be communications centres, command posts, fire positions of the artillery of the reserve, and parts of the 2nd Combat Echelon, or in order to pre-empt a manoeuvre by the enemy in the combat zone, there could be features such as bridges, passes, and so on and so forth. Usually, forces that carry out active combat would move from -- they would be -- they would include anywhere from between a group to a reinforced battalion depending on the purpose of the attack. My group carried out a lot of such attacks, primarily in order to improve the tactical position of the brigade. For instance, such as the attack on Kijevo in October 1993, the attack on the eastern slopes of Igman, where we burned everything in the front -- on the front line and closed off or set off the -- closed off the trenches, attacks on the Guca village and so on, and in this way we would bring our brigade into better tactical position. In addition, we carried out numerous active operations such as diversions at the forward end of the enemy and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there any room for retreat or withdrawal from your front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, practically, we did not -- we could not withdraw. We had a determined defence. We had to hold a determined defence. Any withdrawal would mean the fall of Sarajevo and the cutting off of the territory that was under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which would have a catastrophic effect on both the Army of Republika Srpska and of Republika Srpska itself, so we had to conduct a decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I wish to turn to paragraph 7 of your statement on the same page in both languages. Here you say neither you nor your brigade view these actions as part of a systematic or widespread attack on civilians. Can you tell me if any superior officer or orders ever talked of engaging in a widespread or systematic attack on civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to paragraph 11 of your statement, which is to be found on page 4 in both languages. Here you're talking of training and brochures on the topic of the international law of war and humanitarian law. How often were these trainings undertaken?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: These trainings were undertaken, more often than not, during lull periods and in periods when the intensity of combat was lower which was usually the case in the winter time. They were conducted, if I can give you a complete answer, at the level of the basic unit, either the company or battalion level, and they were -- we received from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army and the main command, we received various brochures and leaflets with photographs and so on. The brunt or the focus of training was the defence, the protection of civilians in wartime, the treatment of enemy prisoners of war, of enemy wounded, what the Red Cross and the red crescent are, what the tasks of humanitarian organisations in that area were, and what our tasks or objectives in relation to that would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What efforts were undertaken to make this material more accessible and understandable to the average soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, as the background, the education background, was different for the various soldiers, the privates would vary differently amongst themselves, but also officers would be at a much higher level of education, so this brochure would have to be adapted and simplified and everything would be clarified with the help of various photographs and figures so that even those who were least educated could understand the gist of the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can ask a follow-up. If we can turn to page 30 of your statement, which is on page 7 in the English and page 8 in the Serbian. Now here, sir, you talk about the fact that most of your brigade was from the reserve force and had very few active servicemen. What steps were taken specifically to train the reserve component or reserve officers during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the Main Staff of the VRS really tried to send active duty personnel so that in 1993, the brigade received four officers that were trained active duty officers. The commander of the brigade, a lieutenant-colonel who had just completed the academy, a company commander, and a platoon commander who had graduated from the military high school. Now, in view of the fact that most of our soldiers, most of our officers were officers in reserve, it was necessary to conduct training at the level of the platoon, at the level of the company, battalion, and brigade. Within the brigade, the level was usually at the -- at the company and platoon level. The commanders of the lower level units would be organised and grouped according to special -- military specialty. For instance, infantry or the mortar group or various different weapons groups. So at the corps level, in addition to company commanders, the corps would insist on the -- of the training of officers for the 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, and there would also be training for various other specialties. In addition, in the Rajko Balac barracks there was additional training organised for officers, and some officers were trained in the army of Yugoslavia. For instance, one of my commanders was sent to Pancevo where he would be trained in order to make it possible for him to carry out the military tasks assigned to him in a more professional way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to paragraph 18 of the statement and page 5 in English and page 6 in the Serbian. In this paragraph, you talk about the ABiH side deploying military weapons in apartments and high rises, especially in Hrasnica. Can you tell me if civilians were still present in these areas where the ABiH positioned their military?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly. As an example, in Hrasnica there were two high-rise buildings, two skyscrapers, and there were machine-guns emplaced in one flat, a couple of storeys under that or above that there were families living. Then at the front line of their defence, the forward line of their defence, they used on a large scale the basements of private houses where Hrasnica is concerned. Also positions for 82- and 120- mm mortar. To prevent that, we undertook this -- the commanders of brigades actually asked the UNPROFOR observers to resolve such matters because we wanted to avoid the situation of having to fire at civilians. So on the other hand, we informed the corps command, which through its liaison officer, intervened with the UNPROFOR command for such practices, such negative practices to be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to paragraph 19 on both versions on the same page. Here you identify a document, 1D02050.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up that document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we see that the document is dated the 5th of August 1994. And focusing on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll need the second page in English, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the bottom of the document, sir, you propose certain targets of the ABiH to be struck, and the last entry is for the Aleksa Santic primary school in Hrasnica, and it's noted there, "shell production." How did you obtain this information on the use of the school in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We obtained this information from defectors from Hrasnica. This was a daily practice. They defected in groups via the river, Zeljeznica, also the forest. Secondly, we were informed by intelligence bodies through the corps command. In Hrasnica, in the primary school Aleksa Santic, in addition to producing shells in apart of the school - because this is a large facility, a large building - they also trained the Special Police units of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can now turn to P06618, and I would ask for page 3 in e-court. If we could zoom in a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the area or neighbourhood which is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: What do you mean do I recognise the area? I recognise the photograph. This is Hrasnica. This is the school in Hrasnica. That is the Aleksa Santic school.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please ask the witness to speak into the microphone, we cannot hear him properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, one second, please. Witness, could you please speak into the microphone? Otherwise the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a photograph of Hrasnica and I know this entire area, this is my area. I don't know how I could show you. Is this the pointer which I can use? Yes. So this is the workers' home in Hrasnica. This is the Aleksa Santic primary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Could you please wait for a second and follow the instructions to be given by Mr. Ivetic, otherwise we have difficulties in following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, with the assistance of the usher, could you please encircle the entire school grounds of the Aleksa Santic school that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This circled in blue, that is the Aleksa Santic primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the information available to your brigade? Were all three structures that you have now circled being used by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, according to our information, in this part of the school -- can I encircle that? Okay. So in this part of the school, which is in the east part, on this photograph, they produced shells. They manufactured shells. In the central part there was a police school. And to this end, this -- with the flat roof, that was the gym of the school, of the Aleksa Santic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that you mark for us with an X which structure you've just identified that was being used for the production of shells by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This. This one, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this photograph as marked by the witness be introduced as the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 3 of document P6618 as marked by the witness receives number D561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have knowledge of where the aerial bomb, that was fired in April of 1995, landed near the Aleksa Santic school?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please increase the volume, step up the volume? I can't hear properly. So the shell landed here where it is written G10, and to the left a bit. Around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is that knowledge based upon?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We were executing combat activities. The 2nd Sarajevo Brigade was attacked on the third day intensively from the Hrasnica area. The compound of the Famos company was attacked by forces three battalions strong. The bomb was fired on the third day. I didn't know that that would be fired, but I noticed a big explosion and a huge smoke rising and I looked to see where that could be. And it was my assessment, as I already stated at the trial in Mr. Karadzic's case and I so confirm here, I assess that it fell approximately in the area of the target, some 20 or 30 metres away from it actually. This bomb has between 105 and 107 kilograms of explosives. On impact it ejects about 550 cubic metres of earth. It displaces, rather. And there is a huge cloud of dust and smoke which is over 100 metres in diameter because it fell as -- on an inhabited place. From my observation post I could not notice the crater which is usually up to 18 metres in diameter and up to five metres deep. I couldn't see that. I had to make my own assessment on the basis of the smoke so -- by immediate observation. So I also asked the command of the corps by operative lines that. They told me that the Igman Brigade had fired an aerial bomb on the Aleksa Santic school building in Hrasnica. So these are the two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now return to D559 and page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I read in the transcript that the bomb had between 105 and 107 kilograms of explosives which is -- I wonder whether that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you tell us, Witness, what the -- how many kilograms of explosives were in this aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As this was a contact bomb, aerial bomb, intended for medium and strong fortified facilities, the bomb itself weighs, Your Honour, about 250 kilograms, depending on the type of the bomb, the newer ones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. I only asked for the explosives. All the rest was not asked. So I do understand that the weight was 250 kilograms. And then you say depending on the type of bomb. What bomb was used in this case? Was it a 250 kilograms or it was a different one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my assessment the bomb which was used was a contact action bomb weighing 250 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by assessment? I mean, on the basis of what did you assess that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the explosion, the smoke, and the displaced earth by the bomb at the moment of impact, at the moment of explosion. It fell about 9.00 in the morning so that this could be easily seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the exact point of impact was also determined by you on the basis of the smoke and the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. And also because I was unable to see the actual crater, because the buildings in between were an obstacle. I couldn't see the crater from the observation post where I was. So it was the smoke column which is actually the basis of my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, around that time, what was the closest, so, well, let's say the days after the explosion, what was the closest you ever came to the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what -- what was the closest distance, was it 500 metres, was it 1 kilometre, was it 300 metres from the point of impact that you were when assessing where the bomb impacted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my observation post, that was between 3 and 3.5 kilometres, between 3.000 and 3500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I'd like to focus our attention on paragraph 21 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk about Hrasnica and Dobrinja as having no exclusively civilian zones where enemy units or firing positions were not located. According to your JNA training, was such a placement of ABiH units in accord with the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We were taught in our military schools that he who plans, organises, and executes combat actions in an inhabited place shall remove civilians from the combat zone. Therefore, the existence of weapons and of personnel in civilian zones is impermissible under international law. That is what we were taught and that is an obvious example of the violation of international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you say violation, violation by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: By the adversary, the opposite side, the Muslims. That was the 104th Brigade of the Army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 in English and page 9 in Serbian and look at paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You here are talking about snipers and the training and you mention Exhibit P04463.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have P04463 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would ask you, sir, if you could please tell us what did your brigade use snipers for, and for this purpose if you can refer to the document where applicable to explain the use of snipers by your brigade, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, my brigade held a part of the front towards the slopes of Treskavica, Bjelasnica, Igman, then a part towards the inhabited places Hrasnica, Butmir, and initially at the outset of the war also Dobrinja. We had 17 sniper rifles, 7.6 mm. We used most of these snipers outside inhabited places. As far as I can recall, I only had two sniper rifles in the river Zeljeznica where their potential could be used and that is so -- is confirmed by my order of the 31st of July 1994. In item 5 of this order I said in selecting the area, the position for snipers, deploy in places outside inhabited places, the Igman area, and see that the protection possibilities of our units are favourable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, sir. One moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. The interpreters are unable to follow your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps the microphone could be directed towards him. I believe they're having difficulty with the microphone as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's it. The microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please slowly proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand. Thank you. In item 3, I ordered the following: In order to ensure as economical and effective a performance by snipers, including paired snipers against enemy personnel, and then in parentheses I stress officers and soldiers, and taking into account the very limited quantity of ammunition, undertake new preparations in respect of the selection of positions, in brackets places for snipers, and at targets and the avoidance of negative counter-effects. This means that sniper fire should not be used where enemy forces can fire back by opening fire on our units, columns of motor vehicles and people, civilians, especially children, and on roads used by buses for transport to Ilidza, Lukavica, and Kasindol. In item 4 I stress combat snipers should be issued with precise tasks, the place, the time, the mode of combat, mode of combat control, and method of reporting the results. Excuse me, in combat, primarily use weapons with silencers and shoot with precision. Use ammunition sparingly. If you will allow me, I should just like to clarify with a couple of sentences what I actually meant and wanted to achieve by this order, and I wanted exclusively to order that only important enemy personnel, which is soldiers and officers, should be targeted. There is no mention of civilians at all. Secondly, I put snipers outside inhabited places because they operated 30 bullets per minute, and the distances in inhabited places are small, in places -- in places even under 100 metres, so that as all units had automatic weapons, where one rifle can eject 120 bullets a minute, and a group of shooters 360 bullets per minute, so the probability of hitting targets by ordinary automatic weapons, then by snipers, is much greater than by snipers. Snipers are used outside inhabited places, at distances up to 800 metres in good visibility conditions, and, Your Honour, perhaps I should also add that this sniper achieves the best results when the trajectory of the bullet, of the -- does not exceed the elevation of the target, which is called the range, the clear range. This range, when it comes to targets such as a soldier in a trench, is 350 metres. When it comes to targets up to 50 centimetres, the range is 450 metres. So that I believe that I properly instructed and correctly used my snipers, and in keeping with international law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just for the sake of the record ask you the document you have read out and commented upon is from the 30th of July 1994, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because earlier you said on the order of the 31st of July. But that must be a slip on -- of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, a slip of the tongue. It's one day. It doesn't really substantially change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could move to another topic, sir. Did you have occasion to learn of a tunnel under the Butmir airport.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the types of things being transited through the tunnel, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: According to our information, the priority users -- those who predominantly used the tunnel were the military the police and members of the government, and also weapons, fuels, and ammunition when it comes to materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the capacity of the transit through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We found out about the tunnel towards the end of summer 1993 or in the autumn of 1993. We did not know exactly how long the tunnel was. We assessed at the time that it was 800 metres long, whereas the actual length was 720. Okay, we were mistaken there. Defectors told us that it was about 150 metres wide -- long, and 100 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked, and in this respect I also complete the record, about the capacity of the transit through the tunnel. Now, you were describing us exactly length or measurements, but that was about capacity that you were asked. Could you tell us what was the capacity of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. The capacity in our assessment was about 4.000 men a day, people a day, on condition that it is used only at night, and about 25 tonnes of materiel could be also transferred through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the basis of your assessment of the capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was simple to. It is actually elementary school arithmetic. It is simple to calculate. If you will allow me, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the tunnel, as I said, was about 800 metres long. Units of the army, of all armies in the world who move on foot at night move on average 2 to 4 kilometres per hour. In our assessment we soldiers, we in the military, always opt for the worst case scenario, so in this case we took it that they were moving at the speed of two kilometres per hour because of the mud, because of the poor visibility, because of the small elevation of the slope, the gradient, et cetera. So this is one element of the calculation. And when we have these elements, if we put them in proportion and in an equation with one unknown, 2.000 metres in 60 seconds are actually covered by the soldiers -- in 60 minutes, I apologise. So 800 metres will be covered by X minutes. So once that equation is solved, it turns out that the time to pass through the tunnel was 24 minutes. We said that it was used only at night. If we say that night lasts on the average ten hours during 24 hours, so if we then take off eight hours for the personnel and two hours for the materiel and equipment of the ten hours, then 88 hours times 60 minutes, that is 480 minutes. When we divide that by 24 minutes, which is for one tour of soldiers to pass, the result is 20 trips or journeys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever tested this or was the assessment ever verified as to speed or was it just a theoretical approach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. These were practically -- practical tests. This is written in our manuals. We march with brigades with thousands of kilometres. I'm an infantry officer. We have tested this in practice time and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I mean verified on the basis of the specifics of this tunnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, when we learned from -- what we learned from Muslims, our assessments verified, were proven true. Actually, I have not finished what I started. So 20 trips could be made but on condition -- because of the height of the tunnel, let us say that the distance between the soldiers with their sidearms was 2 metres. So 400 people could pass through the tunnel in 24 hours. But the unit is never grouped one by one. That would be a column 16 kilometres long. That is why 50 per cent of this time is dedicated to the creation of interval, so spaces between columns. Between every group of 400 people, which is the strength of a battalion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupted you for a good reason because what I wanted to find out is whether it was just calculations or how it was verified, and if you would -- could tell us how it was verified, then please proceed. If not, then I've heard sufficiently of your theoretical arithmetic approach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was verified because we received information from people who had actually passed through the tunnel, and covered it even in shorter times later when it was illuminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have three more questions in direct to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could, I leave it to you, perhaps together with Mr. Mladic whether -- well, a short question doesn't mean that we have a short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think you would be able to guide the witness in such a way that we could finish in the next five minutes, then it's okay. Otherwise, we'll have to take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think since it's the break for the end of the day we could probably just wait until tomorrow and then we'll be sure to finish without overtaxing the translators too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we finish tomorrow. Three more questions to be expected tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we will adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, but I also instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 15th of July, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of July, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 25
